title: Straight Pool (14.1) Rules Explained: How to Play Pool's Classic Game
description: Learn how straight pool (14.1 continuous) works: call shots, the re-rack, scoring and foul penalties, plus why it makes you better at every pool game.
body:
Imagine running 100 balls in a row without missing. Now imagine the pros who do it for fun. Straight pool, also called 14.1 continuous, is the game that gave the Mosconi Cup its name, and it is one of the best ways to learn real pool skill. With Mosconi Cup week almost here (Orlando, November 27-30), it is a perfect time to learn how the game works.

What is straight pool?

Straight pool is a call-shot game played with all 15 object balls and the cue ball. There are no solids or stripes. Any object ball can be your target, and each ball you legally pocket after calling it is worth one point. The first player to reach an agreed total wins. Pros often play to 100 or more, while friendly games might go to 50 or even 25.

How a game starts

The 15 balls are racked in a triangle. The player who breaks must follow the opening-break rules of the rule set being used. Under World Pool-Billiard Association (WPA) style rules, the breaker either calls a ball and pocket and makes it, or drives the cue ball into the pack and then drives at least two object balls to a cushion. Miss those requirements and it is a breaking foul, which costs two points and can give the opponent the choice of re-racking.

Calling your shots

Before each shot you call the ball and the pocket. Lucky bounces do not count, so if you pocket a different ball, your turn ends and the ball stays down. Bank shots, combinations and caroms all count, as long as you called them clearly. If you play casually, an honest nod of the cue toward the pocket is fine, but agree on this with your opponent first.

The re-rack: the heart of the game

Here is the clever part. When you pocket down to one object ball left on the table, the other 14 are racked again in the triangle with the apex spot left open. Then play continues. The goal is to pocket the last loose ball in a way that sends the cue ball to the rack and breaks open a cluster of balls for your next shot.

That is why straight pool rewards planning. You are always thinking two or three shots ahead.

Fouls and penalties

Straight pool scoring uses penalties instead of ball in hand. Under WPA-style rules:

  • An ordinary foul costs one point, and your turn ends.
  • Three fouls in a row cost an extra 15 points on top of the usual penalty. After a second consecutive foul, players are warned.
  • A breaking foul costs two points.

Details can differ between leagues and local rules, so always check which set is being used. New to fouls in other games? Our pool fouls guide covers ball in hand.

Why straight pool makes you better

Even if you mostly play 8-ball or 9-ball, a few frames of straight pool teach habits that carry over:

  • Position play: every shot must set up the next. Read more in our cue ball control guide.
  • Patience: you learn when a safety is smarter than a risky shot. See safety play for beginners.
  • Pattern thinking: clusters and key balls are everywhere in all pool games.

The legend behind the name

Willie Mosconi, the man the Mosconi Cup is named after, was a straight pool master. He is remembered for a famous 526-ball run in 1954. Read the story in our Willie Mosconi guide.

Key terms to know

  • Break ball: the ball you save to open the re-racked pack. Good players plan it several shots early.
  • Key ball: a ball that lets you reach the break ball with perfect position.
  • Cluster: balls touching each other. Spread them out early, before they block your run.
  • Safety: a shot that leaves your opponent with no good option. In straight pool it is part of normal play, not a sign of weakness.

Common beginner mistakes

Rushing the first ball. Many new players pocket the easiest ball without asking where the cue ball will end up. Slow down and pick the shot that leaves a simple next shot.

Forgetting the last ball. Leaving the final loose ball in a spot where you cannot reach the pack wastes the re-rack. Think about it when five or six balls remain.

Ignoring clusters. Balls stuck together are hard to separate later. Use a shot or two early to break them apart while you still have easy options.

How the pros play it today

Straight pool is not as common on the big televised tours as nine-ball, but it remains a respected test of skill, and strong players still compete in it at special events and leagues. Many pros say that practicing 14.1 sharpens their cue ball control for every other game. You can watch top players at the Mosconi Cup, and our Mosconi Cup format guide is a good next read.

Try it this weekend

  1. Rack all 15 balls and play to 25 points with a friend.
  2. Call every shot, pocket and all.
  3. Re-rack when one ball is left, and try to use that last ball to break the pack.

Want to watch the pros instead? Check the Mosconi Cup 2026 hub, and find a game near you on our this weekend page.
